title: How Do You Know When You Love Someone? 16 Real Signs
h1: How Do You Know When You Love Someone? 16 Real Signs It's More Than a Crush
description: How do you know when you love someone? Learn 16 signs that separate love from infatuation, how love changes over time and simple ways to say it out loud.
keyword: how do you know when you love someone
excerpt: Love feels different from a crush. These 16 signs help you tell the difference, plus how to say it when you're ready.
intro:
Falling for someone can feel like a fog and a spotlight at the same time. You cannot stop thinking about them, yet you are not quite sure what the feeling is. Is it a crush, chemistry, comfort or the real thing? There is no blood test for love, but there are patterns that show up again and again when affection deepens into something lasting.

Below are 16 signs that help answer the question “how do you know when you love someone?” Some are about the giddy early stage, others about the steadier love that grows over time. You will also find the difference between love and infatuation, and gentle advice on saying it out loud.
body:
Love vs. infatuation: what's the difference?

Infatuation is fast and intense. It is fueled by novelty, attraction and a lot of imagination about who someone might be. Love tends to grow more slowly and is built on knowing who someone actually is, flaws included. A useful test: infatuation is mostly about how a person makes you feel; love includes genuine care about how they feel, even when it costs you something.

Both can be wonderful, and infatuation often comes first. The signs below move roughly from early-stage feelings to deeper ones.

Early signs you are falling for someone

1. They stand out in any room

You can be surrounded by interesting people and still find your attention drifting back to one person. Their voice, their laugh, the way they tell a story: they register differently.

2. You can't stop thinking about them

They pop into your head when you wake up, while you are making coffee and right before sleep. You rehearse things to tell them and save up small moments to share.

3. You notice their quirks, and like them

The odd way they eat fries, the song they always hum, the dramatic sigh before answering a question. Little habits that would bore you in anyone else become oddly endearing.

4. Your emotions ride a rollercoaster

A text from them can make your whole afternoon. A slow reply can sink it. Early love is famously moody, and those swings are a sign of how much the connection matters to you.

5. Everything reminds you of them

A song on the radio, a menu item, a meme, a street name. Your brain keeps linking the world back to them.

6. You talk about them constantly

Your friends have heard the story about their dog four times. You find ways to mention them in conversations that have nothing to do with them.

Signs your feelings are deepening

7. You want to talk to them every day

Not out of anxiety, but because sharing your day with them makes it feel complete. Good news and bad news alike, they are the first person you want to tell.

8. Time together feels easy

You enjoy big dates, but you also love doing nothing together: groceries, errands, a quiet night in. Comfortable silence is a strong sign of real closeness.

9. You see their flaws and still choose them

The early idealized picture fades and you see the real person: their impatience, their messy car, their tendency to run late. You still want them. That shift from “perfect” to “real and still wonderful” is one of the clearest markers of love.

10. You get curious about their world

You start learning about their hobbies, listening to their music or reading about their job, not to impress them, but because what matters to them now matters to you.

11. You want to know their people

Meeting their friends and family feels important, and you want those people to like you. You make an effort to fit into their life, not just have them fit into yours.

12. You're willing to compromise

You find yourself meeting halfway on plans, chores and decisions without keeping score. Their happiness genuinely feels like part of your own.

13. You do kind things without being asked

Picking up their favorite snack, filling their gas tank, sending a note before a big meeting. Love shows up in small, unprompted acts of care.

14. You picture a future with them

Holidays, trips, even where you might live. When your mental plans for next year automatically include them, your heart is telling you something.

15. Your ex barely crosses your mind

Old relationships stop occupying space. You are not comparing anymore; you are simply focused on what you have now.

16. You want to grow, partly because of them

Love often inspires you to be more patient, more honest or more open. Not because they demanded it, but because you want to be a good partner to them.

Tip: If you are still unsure, try this question: “If they needed me during an inconvenient week, would I want to show up?” A wholehearted yes points toward love rather than just attraction.

How love changes over time

One reason people doubt their feelings is that love does not stay the same. The early rush, sometimes called passionate love, is full of excitement, longing and constant thoughts about the other person. Over months and years, many couples move into what is often called companionate love: deep friendship, trust, shared routines and a quieter but sturdier kind of affection.

Neither stage is more real than the other. The shift can feel alarming if you expect the butterflies to last forever, but it is usually a sign the relationship is settling, not fading. Couples keep the spark alive by doing new things together, staying curious about each other and making time for affection and play.

A few questions can help you check in with your feelings at any stage:

  • Do I feel more like myself around them, or less?
  • Do I want good things for them, even things that don't involve me?
  • When we disagree, do I still respect them?
  • Am I glad, overall, that they are in my life?

If your answers are mostly yes, you are likely looking at love, whatever stage it is in. For more on recognizing the feeling, read how do you know you are in love.

Healthy love vs. anxious attachment

Strong feelings are not always healthy ones. It is worth checking that what you feel is love and not fear of losing someone. Signs to pause and reflect include:

  • You feel more anxious than happy most of the time.
  • You change core parts of yourself to keep them interested.
  • You feel you have to earn basic respect or kindness.
  • Your friends and family are worried about how you are treated.

Healthy love feels safe, mutual and steady, even when it is exciting. If you are struggling with anxiety in a relationship, our guide on how to not be insecure is a good place to start, and a licensed therapist can help you sort through bigger patterns.

Simple ways to show someone you love them

Once you recognize the feeling, you will probably want to show it. A few ideas to start with:

  • Listen fully, with your phone away.
  • Remember and ask about the things that matter to them.
  • Say thank you for the small stuff.
  • Leave a short note in their bag or on the mirror.
  • Cook their favorite meal, even badly.
  • Show up for their big days: interviews, recitals, tough appointments.
  • Learn their love language and speak it.
  • Plan a date around something they love.
  • Defend them when they are not in the room.
  • Give them space when they need it, without taking it personally.
  • Celebrate their wins as loudly as your own.
  • Apologize sincerely when you get it wrong.

For many more ideas, browse how to show someone you love them and how to show love through everyday actions.

How to say “I love you” when you're ready

There is no rule for timing. Some couples say it in weeks, others in months. A few guidelines help:

  1. Say it because it's true, not to get a response. Love offered as a test puts pressure on both of you.
  2. Choose a calm, private moment. A quiet walk beats a crowded party or the middle of an argument.
  3. Keep it simple. “I love you” or “I've fallen in love with you” is enough.
  4. Give them room. If they are not ready to say it back, that is not a rejection. People move at different speeds.

If speaking feels too hard, writing can help. Our I love you letters offer examples you can adapt.

The bottom line

You know you love someone when your care for them is steady, specific and real: you see who they are, flaws included, and you still want to show up for them. The butterflies may come and go, but the wish to make their life better tends to stay. Trust that feeling, take your time and, when it is right, tell them.
takeaways: Infatuation is about how someone makes you feel; love includes caring how they feel.
Seeing someone's flaws clearly and still choosing them is a strong sign of love.
Healthy love feels safe and mutual, not constantly anxious.
Say “I love you” because it's true, in a calm moment, without demanding it back.

faq.q: How long does it take to know you love someone?
faq.a: There is no set timeline. Some people feel it within weeks, others after many months. What matters more is whether you know the real person, flaws included, and still feel steady care and commitment. Intense early attraction can grow into love, but it usually takes shared experiences to be sure.

faq.q: What is the difference between love and a crush?
faq.a: A crush is usually fast, intense and based partly on imagination about who someone is. Love develops as you get to know the person and includes caring about their wellbeing, accepting their flaws, compromising and imagining a shared future. Crushes can fade quickly; love tends to deepen.

faq.q: Can you love someone and not be in love with them?
faq.a: Yes. You can love someone deeply as a friend or family member, or still care for an ex, without romantic attraction or the wish to build a romantic life together. Being in love usually includes attraction, emotional intimacy and a desire for partnership.

faq.q: Should I tell someone I love them first?
faq.a: If your feelings are sincere and the relationship feels secure, there is nothing wrong with saying it first. Choose a calm moment, keep it simple and do not demand an immediate response. If they need time, that is normal and not necessarily a sign they do not care.
